pages.text: CLIENT ASSESSMENT AND GOAL SETTING CHAPTER 12 1 | Understand client assessments used by a nutrition coach. 2 | Employ the appropriate assessment forms with clients. 3 | Discuss the importance of setting goals with clients. 4 | Describe SMART goals. ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 253 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

CHAPTER 12 | Client Assessment and Goal Setting ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 254 Clients seek the support of a nutrition coach for many reasons, such as improving energy, supporting overall health, enhancing performance, managing stress, or feeling more confident in their eating habits. Every client’s goals, background, and circumstances are unique. Before building any kind of program or beginning the behavior change process together, a nutrition coach and client engage in a collaborative assessment process. This is an opportunity to: • Learnabout the client’s motivations and priorities in their own words. • Explore realistic, personally meaningful goals. • Create a plan that supports sustainable progress. Assessments are not tests or judgments; they are tools to help both the client and coach understand where the client is starting and how they would like to grow. ASSESSMENTS When building rapport with a client, a nutrition coach can perform a variety of assessments to gather information and establish a baseline. These assessments are always optional and conducted with informed consent. Types of assessment include: • Personal: demographic information, preferred communication methods, and initial goals • Physical: measurements that the client chooses to track, such as weight, height, or strength markers. • Health: current and past health history via a health questionnaire. • Physical activity: current activity patterns, preferences, and barriers. • Photographic: client-approved images to track visible changes, if desired. • Behavioral: nutrition and lifestyle patterns, often through food diaries or journaling. • Psychological: the client’s motivations, confidence, and readiness for change. PERSONAL ASSESSMENTS Personal assessments begin the process of data collection, starting with basic information such as a client’s address, contact information, emergency contact, and what the client hopes to achieve. A client can fill out a form for these questions, or a coach can sit and speak with the client to gather the information. ASSESSMENTS: The evaluation or estimation of the nature, quality, or ability of an individual. PERSONAL ASSESSMENTS: The collection of demographic and initial data from a client.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 255 When conducted in person or virtually, these conversations should feel open and respectful, allowing the client to share only what they are comfortable with. The goal is to establish trust, not to collect every possible detail. PHYSICAL ASSESSMENT Physical assessments can offer objective data about a client’s current status. Examples include: • Height • Weight (if the client wishes to track it) • Body composition (e.g., muscle mass, body fat percentage, if available and agreed upon) • Circumference measurements • Strength, flexibility, or endurance benchmarks Not all clients will want or need all of these measurements. Coaches should explain what each metric means, how it will be used, and offer alternatives. For example, a client who does not wish to track weight (or that metric doesn’t align with their stated goals) may prefer focusing on energy levels, performance goals, or lifestyle habits. If certain tools such as skinfold calipers are not available, alternative measures can be used. Free online body composition or caloric calculators are optional resources and should be presented as such, not as requirements. PHYSICAL ASSESSMENTS: Objective data about the client’s physical status. OBJECTIVE DATA: Data collected through observations and actual data, not opinions.

PHYSICAL ASSESSMENT PROS CONS Weight Easy measurement to collect Changes in weight do not explain what is changing Height Most clients will know their height; it is helpful in body composition calculation None Body composition Gives detail on body mass and fat mass May be difficult to calculate if proper tools are not available Circumference measurement Helpful for body composition calculation, easy to track changes Not all clients know how to gather this data, consistency of measurement locations Skinfold measurements Helpful for body composition calculation Most clients won’t have the tool, consistency of measurement locations

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 257 HEALTH ASSESSMENTS Health assessments use a brief, client-completed questionnaire to capture relevant health background. This process helps identify any modifications needed to keep nutrition coaching within scope and safe. The nutrition coach does not diagnose or treat medical conditions. Instead, the coach may ask: • “Do you have any dietary needs or restrictions you’d like me to know about?” • “Are there any foods that cause discomfort or allergic reactions?” • “Do you have any current health considerations that might influence nutrition choices?” If needed, the client can choose to share medical provider information and grant written consent for any communication. All health information must be stored securely and confidentially. PHYSICAL ACTIVITY ASSESSMENTS A client’s current level of physical activity is important for a nutrition coach to properly assess their calorie needs and expenditures. An exercise history questionnaire provides information on current sports, frequency of activity, and level of fitness. HEALTH ASSESSMENTS: Questionnaires used to collect current and past health history from a client.

CHAPTER 12 | Client Assessment and Goal Setting ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 258 PHOTO ASSESSMENTS Photo assessments are optional and client-directed. Using them can help clients see their progress throughout a nutrition coaching program, whether physical, postural, or performance- related. Photos can also boost motivation and celebrate achievements and milestones along the way. Best practices include always obtaining written consent, discussing clothing options that balance comfort, cultural norms, and visibility of changes, allowing the client to decide which angles and how frequently photos are taken, and storing or deleting images according to a clear privacy policy. Figure 12.1 Client Photos. BEHAVIORAL ASSESSMENT Behavioral assessments explore patterns in nutrition, hydration, and lifestyle habits. Clients may use food diaries, meal logs, or other self-tracking methods to reflect on their typical meal patterns and timing, the emotional or situational influences on their eating, and their food access and preparation routines. The aim is understanding, not judgment, and questions should be open-ended and culturally sensitive, such as asking what a typical day of eating looks like for them or how special occasions or travel influence their eating patterns. These conversations can also explore how clients respond to stressors, acknowledging that for many people, food is connected to emotions such as anxiety, stress, sadness, or boredom. The process should remain collaborative and respectful, with a focus on identifying patterns rather than assigning blame. Well-crafted, open-ended questions encourage self- reflection and help clients share their experiences in ways that honor their autonomy.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 259 For example, the coach might ask: Do you eat when you are bored? • “When you’re feeling stressed, anxious, or bored, how does that affect your eating patterns, if at all?” • “How do you typically feel around mealtimes or when you snack?” • “What influences the timing of your first meal each day?” • “Are there certain foods or eating experiences that feel comforting to you? What makes them comforting?” • “Have you noticed any times when eating feels less comfortable or satisfying? What do you think contributes to that?” • “How does your daily schedule or environment affect when and how you eat?” The goal of these conversations is not to diagnose disordered eating or assess mental health, but to understand how food fits into a client’s emotional and practical coping strategies. If a client shares concerns that could be better addressed by another specialist, the nutrition coach can, with the client’s consent, refer them to trusted professionals in their network. This helps ensure the client receives care that is appropriate, effective, and tailored to their needs..

CHAPTER 12 | Client Assessment and Goal Setting ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 260 PSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENTS A nutrition coach is concerned with the psychology of a client’s motivation and readiness to change. Psychological assessments include questions regarding what motivates the client, what they feel distracts them from their progress, and how they feel about their nutrition journey—past and present. Details collected can allow a coach to establish the client’s current stage of change and better tailor their program to keep them motivated. Figure 12.2 The Stages of Change. Pre-Contemplation There is no intention of addressing a behavior. Contemplation They are aware of the need to change but have barriers to overcome to address it. Maintenance They are continuing to do what is needed to maintain the desired behavior. Preparation They have the desire to change and are seeking a way. Action They are taking the necesssary steps to address their behavior and change it. The Stages of Change model can be a helpful conversation tool, but it’s important to acknowledge that progress is not always linear. Clients may revisit earlier stages as life circumstances shift. Key skills during these conversations include expressing empathy through reflective listening, asking open-ended questions to uncover motivations and barriers, and supporting client autonomy in defining next steps. REASSESSMENT Reassessments allow both client and coach to celebrate progress, identify changes in priorities, and adapt the plan. This process should highlight successes, big or small, and explore any barriers without blame. PSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENTS: Questions regarding what motivates the client, what they feel distracts them from their progress, and how they feel about their nutrition journey—past and present. REASSESSMENT: Repeating a previously completed assessment for comparison.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 261 Progress measures can include: • Updated nutrition diaries • Physical assessments • Lifestyle and wellbeing check-ins • Photo assessments Coaches must protect client confidentiality and follow retention guidelines appropriate to their jurisdiction. SETTING GOALS Goal setting is a collaborative process in which the client identifies what matters most to them, and the coach works to break these priorities into clear, achievable steps. Over time, goals may shift as the client’s needs, circumstances, or interests change. They may center on building health- promoting habits, improving energy and mood, enhancing physical function, increasing confidence in food choices, or strengthening community and social engagement. TYPES OF GOALS Many types of goals exist, but nutrition coaches primarily focus on physical, health, and behavior goals, as these are most directly influenced by nutrition and lifestyle. Physical Goals May include functional fitness, strength, flexibility, or endurance. Examples: • Completing a local 5k walk/run • Improving balance to reduce fall risk • Carrying groceries up stairs without fatigue • Being able to do a pull-up Health Goals Health goals focus on well-being and may be related to medical care, but without assuming medical outcomes. Examples include: • Consistently meeting hydration targets • Preparing balanced breakfasts most days • Improving sleep quality through evening routines GOAL SETTING: The process of establishing what someone wishes to achieve and measurable timelines to do it.

CHAPTER 12 | Client Assessment and Goal Setting ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 262 Behavior Goals Behavior goals are those involving a specific behavior change, one the client has control over. Perhaps it is an adjustment to a current behavior or the introduction of a new one. Here are some examples: • Drinking only one cup of coffee per day • Cooking at home three nights per week • Practicing mindful eating at one meal per day • Packing a healthy snack before long workdays • Exercising for 20 minutes every day SMART GOALS SMART goals are specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and timely. Using the outline of a SMART goal when establishing desired program outcomes ensures a clear path to success and makes it easier for a nutrition coach to help the client progress. Figure 12.3 SMART Goals. S A M R T Specific - describe exactly what needs to be accomplished Attainable - are possible to be achieved Measurable - can be evaluated with metrics Realistic - make sense for the client Timely - can be completed in a reasonable and specific amount of time Here’s an example of how to create a SMART goal. The client says they want to eat healthier. The coach can help them turn this into a SMART goal by asking, “What does ‘healthier’ mean to you?” They respond by saying they want to eat three servings of vegetables daily. The coach replies, “When would you like to consistently do this?” The clients responds, “Within the next month.” • Specific: The client eats three servings of vegetables daily. • Measurable: The client can physically measure three servings of vegetables.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 263 • Attainable: It is possible to eat three servings of vegetables a day. • Realistic: The client currently eats vegetables at least every other day and has access to a grocery store to purchase them. • Timely: They want to do this within a month—four weeks. Having a SMART goal is just one part of the goal-setting process that will be repeated with each goal a client sets. GOAL-SETTING STEPS The following are seven steps in the goal-setting process, which is cyclical in nature: 1 Identify what the client wants to achieve and why it matters to them 2 Create a SMART goal together 3 Write the goal(s) down for reference 4 Co-create a plan of action 5 Establish a realistic timeline 6 Take action. 7 Reassess and adjust as needed. The first step in goal setting is critical. A client may have something they want to achieve physically or behaviorally, but if they are not ready or able to commit the time and effort required, the goal may need to be adjusted. When a client brings multiple potential goals, the nutrition coach can help them prioritize by identifying which are most meaningful and achievable in the present moment. For example, a client might say they want to reduce their reliance on blood pressure medication, lose 35 pounds, cut back on nightly ice cream, and decrease their waist measurement by 10 inches. Rather than assuming which goal should come first, the coach can ask open-ended questions such as, “Why is it important for you to reduce or stop taking blood pressure medication?” or “What makes 35 pounds a meaningful target for you?” These questions invite the client to share the motivations behind each goal, whether they come from a healthcare provider’s recommendation, a past experience, or a personal vision for their health and lifestyle.

CHAPTER 12 | Client Assessment and Goal Setting ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 264 By using active listening and motivational techniques, the coach can help the client choose a starting point and shape it into a SMART goal. The resulting plan will likely focus on practical nutrition and lifestyle changes that align with the client’s values and priorities. Writing goals down makes them tangible and provides a reference point for future discussions. A written plan of action with a timeline can help keep the client focused while also leaving room for flexibility. It is normal for setbacks, barriers, and plateaus to arise; adjusting the plan as needed ensures ongoing progress toward the desired outcome. Like assessments, goals should be revisited regularly. They may evolve, be achieved, or be replaced with new ones as circumstances change. Reassessments are not only a way to track progress but also a chance for the coach and client to reconnect, celebrate successes, address challenges, and strengthen the coaching relationship. Figure 12.4 Goal-Setting Steps. Figure out what you want to achieve Create a SMART goal Write it down Create a plan Establish a timeline Act Reassess Goal- Setting Steps
